subunits.title: Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces
subunits.summary: Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are attractions between separate particles. They set boiling point, vapor pressure, and viscosity. Stronger IMFs mean higher boiling point and lower vapor pressure.
concepts: London dispersion forces act between all particles and grow with electron count and polarizability.
Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O, or F, plus a lone pair on N, O, or F in a neighbor.
mistakes: Confusing intermolecular forces with the covalent bonds inside a molecule.
Saying boiling breaks covalent bonds.

cards.front: Which IMF is present in every substance?

cards.back: H bonded to N, O, or F, attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F

mcqs.question: Which substance can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself?
mcqs.explanation: HF has H bonded to F, which also has lone pairs, so molecules hydrogen bond. CH4 and CO2 are nonpolar. HCl has H bonded to Cl, which does not qualify.

mcqs.question: $\ce{Br2}$ has a higher boiling point than $\ce{Cl2}$. The best explanation is that $\ce{Br2}$ has:
choices: C. greater polarizability, so stronger dispersion forces
mcqs.explanation: Both are nonpolar. Br2 has more electrons, so its electron cloud is more polarizable and dispersion forces are stronger. Boiling breaks IMFs, not covalent bonds.

mcqs.question: Which property increases as the strength of intermolecular forces in a liquid increases?
choices: A. Vapor pressure at a fixed temperature
mcqs.explanation: Stronger IMFs hold particles together more tightly, so more energy (a higher temperature) is needed to boil. Vapor pressure, volatility and evaporation rate all decrease.

mcqs.question: The boiling point of $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH3}$ ($-1$ °C) is higher than that of $\ce{CH3CH3}$ ($-89$ °C). The best explanation is that butane has:
choices: B. a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so stronger dispersion forces
mcqs.explanation: Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons, so only dispersion forces act. Butane has more electrons and a larger cloud, so its dispersion forces are stronger.

mcqs.question: Which has the highest boiling point? ($\ce{CH3CH2CH3}$, $\ce{CH3OCH3}$, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$, $\ce{CO2}$; molar masses are all about 44-46 g/mol)
mcqs.explanation: With similar masses, dispersion forces are similar. Only ethanol has O-H, so it hydrogen bonds, the strongest IMF here. Dimethyl ether is polar but cannot hydrogen bond with itself.

mcqs.question: Liquid X has a higher vapor pressure than liquid Y at 25 °C. Which is most likely true?
choices: A. X has stronger IMFs than Y
B. X has weaker IMFs than Y
C. X has a higher boiling point than Y
D. X has more covalent bonds per molecule than Y
mcqs.explanation: Weaker IMFs let more molecules escape into the gas phase, giving a higher vapor pressure and a lower boiling point.

mcqs.question: Which lists the hydrogen halides from lowest to highest boiling point?
mcqs.explanation: HCl, HBr and HI rise with size because dispersion forces grow. HF is highest because it hydrogen bonds, which outweighs the dispersion trend.

mcqs.question: $\ce{Ne}$ (20.18 g/mol) boils at 27 K and $\ce{HF}$ (20.01 g/mol) boils at about 293 K. The best explanation is that:
choices: A. HF has a much greater molar mass
B. HF molecules hydrogen bond, while Ne atoms have only weak dispersion forces
C. Ne has stronger covalent bonds
mcqs.explanation: The molar masses are nearly equal, so dispersion forces are comparable. HF's hydrogen bonding is the major difference.

mcqs.question: A student says $\ce{H2O}$ boils higher than $\ce{H2S}$ because O-H bonds are stronger than S-H bonds. Which evaluation is best?
choices: A. Correct, because boiling breaks covalent bonds
B. Incorrect; boiling overcomes IMFs, and water's hydrogen bonding is stronger than the forces in H2S
C. Correct, because oxygen is more electronegative
D. Incorrect; H2S has stronger dispersion forces than water
mcqs.explanation: Boiling changes the phase and leaves covalent bonds intact. Water's hydrogen bonds are stronger than the attractions between H2S molecules.

mcqs.question: Pentane (72 g/mol) boils at 36 °C and acetone (58 g/mol) boils at 56 °C. Why does acetone, the lighter molecule, boil higher?
choices: A. Acetone hydrogen bonds with itself
B. Acetone's permanent dipole adds dipole-dipole attractions that outweigh pentane's greater dispersion
C. Lower molar mass gives stronger dispersion forces
mcqs.explanation: Acetone has a polar C=O bond but no O-H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself (A is wrong). Its dipole-dipole attractions plus dispersion exceed pentane's dispersion alone.

parts.modelAnswer: Boiling overcomes IMFs while the molecules stay intact, and it absorbs energy.

frqs.modelAnswer: (a) Water vapor. (b) Boiling overcomes IMFs, not bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Which explains the trend from H2S to H2Te?
parts.modelAnswer: Larger atoms give more polarizable electron clouds.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why $\ce{H2O}$ does not fit this trend.

rubric.criterion: Water hydrogen bonds
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the dispersion forces in the others

parts.modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding makes water's IMFs much stronger, raising its boiling point above the trend.

frqs.modelAnswer: (a) Dispersion increases. (b) Hydrogen bonding in water.

subunits.title: Properties of Solids
subunits.summary: Solids are classified by the particles that make them up and the forces holding them together. The four main types are ionic, metallic, covalent network (covalent-network), and molecular. The type of solid determines melting point, hardness, conductivity, and solubility.
concepts: Ionic solids: ions held by electrostatic attraction; high melting point; conduct when molten or dissolved, not as solids.
Metallic solids: metal cations in a sea of delocalized electrons; conduct electricity as solids; malleable.
Covalent network solids: atoms held by an extended network of covalent bonds (diamond, SiO2, SiC); very high melting point; usually nonconductive.
Molecular solids: molecules held by IMFs (ice, dry ice, sugar); low melting point; nonconductive.
Alloys are mixtures of metals with properties often improved over pure metals.
mistakes: Saying ionic solids conduct electricity as solids.
Confusing covalent network solids with molecular solids.
Forgetting that graphite conducts electricity even though it is covalent network.

cards.front: Which solid type conducts electricity as a solid?
cards.back: Metallic (and graphite, a special covalent network)

cards.front: Why does NaCl not conduct as a solid but does when molten?
cards.back: Ions are locked in the lattice; melting frees them to move

mcqs.question: Which type of solid has the highest melting point in general?
mcqs.explanation: Covalent network solids (diamond, SiO2) require breaking many strong covalent bonds, so their melting points are extremely high — often higher than ionic solids.

mcqs.question: Which type of solid conducts electricity in the solid state?
mcqs.explanation: Metals have delocalized electrons that move freely. Ionic solids need to be melted or dissolved to conduct.

mcqs.question: Dry ice (solid CO2) is best classified as a:
mcqs.explanation: CO2 molecules are held together by London dispersion forces, not by an extended covalent network.

mcqs.question: Which property is typical of ionic solids?
mcqs.explanation: Ionic lattices shatter when layers shift; strong electrostatic forces give high melting points.

mcqs.question: Diamond and graphite are both made of carbon. Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
choices: A. Graphite has a lower melting point
B. Graphite has delocalized electrons in its layered structure; diamond's electrons are all in localized sigma bonds
mcqs.explanation: In graphite each C is sp2 hybridized; the remaining p electron is delocalized across the layer, allowing conduction. Diamond's sp3 carbons use all four valence electrons in bonds.

mcqs.question: Which is NOT a property of metallic solids?
mcqs.explanation: Metals deform rather than shatter because the delocalized electron sea lets cation layers slide past each other.

mcqs.question: SiO2 melts at ~1700 °C while CO2 sublimes at -78 °C. The best explanation is:
choices: A. SiO2 has stronger covalent bonds within molecules
B. SiO2 is a covalent network solid; CO2 is molecular with only dispersion forces
mcqs.explanation: SiO2 is an extended covalent network; melting requires breaking many Si-O bonds. CO2 melting only overcomes weak dispersion forces.

mcqs.question: Brass is an alloy of Cu and Zn. Why is brass harder than pure copper?
choices: A. Zn atoms are larger and disrupt the Cu lattice, preventing layers from sliding
B. Zn reacts with Cu to make an ionic solid
C. Zn has more delocalized electrons
D. Brass is a covalent network
mcqs.explanation: Different-sized atoms in the metal lattice distort the layers, making deformation harder — the basis of substitutional alloy strengthening.

mcqs.question: A solid melts at 801 °C, does not conduct when solid, but conducts when molten. It dissolves in water. Which type of solid is it most likely?
mcqs.explanation: High melting point + nonconductive as solid + conductive when molten = classic ionic solid (NaCl melts at 801 °C).

mcqs.question: A solid is insoluble in water, does not conduct as a solid or when molten, and melts above 3000 °C. Best classification?
mcqs.explanation: Extremely high melting point, no conductivity (no free charges), insoluble — consistent with a covalent network like diamond or SiC.

subunits.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
subunits.summary: The three common phases of matter differ in particle spacing, motion, and order. Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but flow; gases fill their container. Phase changes involve heat but not temperature change at the transition.
concepts: Heating curves show plateaus at melting and boiling points.
Heat during a phase change = n × ΔH (fusion or vaporization).
Heat without a phase change = m × c × ΔT.
Sublimation is solid → gas; deposition is gas → solid.
mistakes: Using m c ΔT during a phase change.
Thinking temperature changes during melting or boiling.

subunits.title: Ideal Gas Law
subunits.summary: The ideal gas law combines Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws: PV = nRT. Ideal gas behavior assumes no IMFs and point-like particles. Related laws include Dalton's partial pressures, Graham's effusion, and the combined gas law.
concepts: Use Kelvin, not Celsius.
Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of partial pressures.
Mole fraction × total pressure = partial pressure.
Graham's law: rate ratio = sqrt(M2/M1).
mistakes: Using °C in PV = nRT.
Mixing units of R (atm vs kPa vs J).
Forgetting that STP is 0 °C and 1 atm for molar volume 22.4 L.

subunits.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
subunits.summary: KMT explains gas behavior with five assumptions: gases are mostly empty space, particles move randomly, collisions are elastic, no IMFs between particles, and average kinetic energy depends only on temperature. Average KE = (3/2)kT per molecule or (3/2)RT per mole.
concepts: Average KE depends only on T (in Kelvin), not on identity of gas.
At the same T, all gases have the same average KE.
Heavier gases have slower average speeds.
Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions broaden and shift right with temperature.
mistakes: Thinking heavier gases have more KE at the same T.
Forgetting to convert T to Kelvin.

cards.front: At the same T, which is the same for all gases?
Effect of higher T on Maxwell-Boltzmann curve
cards.back: Broader and shifted right (higher average speed)

mcqs.question: At the same temperature, the average kinetic energy of H2 and O2 is:
mcqs.explanation: Average KE depends only on T.

mcqs.explanation: Higher T spreads the distribution and raises average speed.

mcqs.explanation: u_rms ∝ 1/√M; He (4) is lighter than Ne (20).

mcqs.question: Two gases at the same T have the same average KE. Which has more momentum?
